title: Why did Steven Spielberg falter in the 2010s?

commenti.body: Good question, and it's interesting you cite the 2020s as a comeback when West Side Story and Fablemans did poorly at the box office. Critically acclaimed yes, but it adds a layer to whether it's really what people want to watch. Reading a few articles cited in the Fablemans wikipedia, it seems that "prestige" film is on the downturn for audiences. For me personally I don't really connect with Spielbergs almost sappy kind of feel-good tales anymore. That's all I saw in ads for Fablemans. West Side Story was a similar nostalgia-fueled romp through memory lane wrapped up in modern production values. That's possibly not what you want to discuss here as I'm sure they were technically good movies, but i wonder if lumping his output into decades is an accurate representation of his evolution as a director. Seems to me like he's rather consistent, as he either teeters on wide-eyed fantasy/sci-fi adventures or dramatic period pieces aka the "prestige" films that win oscars. To me his style has always been a bit commercial, but in a way that's completely his own style and today feels like a template. That mostly why I'm not for saying the 2020s is a return to better form, but I'm not a huge film nerd just a random guy so..

I agree with your post. I’ve talked to my friends about how Spielberg has made some of my favorite and also some of the most boring movies I’ve seen, the 2010s period soured me on him for a long time. Sometimes directors lose their juice once the creative box that focused their strengths gets too big or runs empty.

It’s hard enough to make one blockbuster and the fact he essentially did it for 30 years and only recently started having kinda mid movies is just normal I think.

with west side story he had a specific box to play inside instead of completely changing everything so I think that’s why it feels like older Spielberg, lets him use his strengths and the small changes he did either worked better (the Hispanic representation) or didn’t cause enough of a negative to really be worth mentioning (moving the “Cool” fight earlier in the movie)

I know we’re grading Spielberg on a different scale, but I think like 98% of directors would sign up for the level of commercial and critical success Spielberg had in the 2010s in a heartbeat. 

This is purely personal preference and has absolutely nothing to do with the artistic merit of the films, but Ready Player One and Lincoln are two of my favorite Spielberg films to revisit, and for wildly different reasons too.

I always felt from TinTin onward Spielberg has mostly been doing projects that feel much closer to his heart. Not saying that sentimentality or personal passion isn't something he did in the past (movies like Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan and Munich are a testament to that) but it definitely feels like he doesn't particularly care about having a hit over doing something that he enjoys making. Even Ready Player One, no matter how you feel the quality of that movie is, shows Spielberg trying to reconnect to his past. But at the end of the day I don't think he's aiming for broad appeal anymore, just making movies he'd like to see and if they make money they make money.

Also critically acclaimed by his industry pals and media stooges who have a financial interest in rehabilitating his image after a run of mediocre, bland movies 

He’s prolific and that obviously impacts the quality of his oeuvre but I’d say he hasn’t done anything close to great since Munich or Catch Me If You Can, whichever one was first

He made a lot of dad movies that seemed stuffy. Then you watch the actual film and realize that it's better than you thought it was gonna be. I think *Tintin* was his only true triumph in the 10s, and it's pretty slept on in America.

Honestly Spielberg has made some crappy movies. I grew up with them but after getting exposed to film in my later 20s I can’t get over the grandiosity of them. Saving private Ryan is good but it’s not the best war movie by any means. And good lord the camera focusing on Tom hanks hands and then panning to everyone’s faces…it’s like I GET IT! Woody from toy story has shell shock.

I couldn’t get over the strange dialogue in Jaws. Idk I just think it’s one of those things where as the dust settles people will reframe his work. I love the Indiana Jones stuff but I just hate the whole “this is so serious the academy will love this” vibe his films have.

Who the hell is reevaluating War of the Worlds, it was a terrible remake and the changes they did make made even less sense.

I think Spielberg's problem is that he is so prolific as it seems like he enjoys the whole movie making process, so yea there could be some clunkers in there.  Compare that with someone like James Cameron who people will say does not have a miss, which OK, but he also has only done like 8 movies over 40 years.  

One explanation could be that the 2010's was the Marvel decade and with so many resources going into one product there might have been less talent into all the other projects.
He’s made very few movies that are “so serious.” Like zero since Munich and very few outside of the 90s, which was a decade where he made Jurassic Park and Hook ffs.

It's like he was pandering to his past. He made great films that propelled blockbuster filmmaking and brought a lot of technical advancements in cinema, he might have felt he had to continue doing that. So he made films like Tintin and Ready Player One. He was also famous for making inspiring stories based on true events, so he made Bridge of Spies and Lincoln. And these movies are fine, I loved Bridge and Lincoln but it felt like he was going through the motions. All of them were proficient but none of them became memorable compared to his earlier works. 

I think now he's past trying to deliver hits and just making what he wants. West Side Story and The Fablemans were better than any of his 2010s works.

I think Bridge of Spies was phenomenal. I have a soft spot for espionage flicks and this hit most of the right notes for what I look for in that genre. It maybe was a bit sentimental toward the end (aren’t all his movies) but I hope it eventually has a reappraisal as I feel it deserves to stand out as a strong moment in an otherwise dull decade for him.

Yeah it’s purely fiction and VERY dour but it’s one of his better films of this century in my opinion.

The short answer is he has become more of a Movie Mogul than a film director. His earlier films are largely passion projects. Almost everything since 2010 are more product than stories he seems inspired by. It’s a Spielberg product, same cinematography, same tone, often same actors or actors everyone knows. It’s great for the studios bottom line I suppose, but not very engaging as a viewer. I was excited for Fablemen’s but the end result was a jumbled narrative that really didn’t know what film it wanted to be.

The problem is we expect more from Spielberg. All those 2010 films are fantastic films, but they're all compared to Raiders and Schindler and Jurrassic and Jaws and ET. No other filmmaker's work gets compared to those films. He has a lot to live up to. 

The best argument you can make is that they're not challenging films.

Terminal was a Capraesque story that could have been amazing if it didn't have Tom Hanks. Spielberg has a long history of introducing new actors to the screen, and if the film had starred a relatively unknown East European actor (think Christoph Waltz or Mark Rylance) instead of Tom Hanks with a fake accent, then we'd probably think of it as more than just "a nice movie." But Spielberg played it safe by casting Hanks, who was never convincing as an immigrant.

War of the Worlds is one of Spielberg's biggest disappointments. He delivered a competent sci-fi thriller, but any director could have done that. For Spielberg to tackle an end of the world disaster film post 9/11, it should have been truly dark and horrifying - like beyond Schindler/Private Ryan levels of terror. It should have been an outright horror movie, but Spielberg played it safe and the result was meh. It's odd how no major directors make horror movies, even ones that earned their fame making horror. Hitchcock showed how turning to horror at the height of your fame could be effective. War of the Worlds should have been his Psycho.

Tintin was interesting because it was his first animated film, and suddenly he had complete control over the camera movements and blocking and that made for great storytelling, but in the end it was a watered-down Indiana Jones type of movie. Not really challenging.

The BFG was aimed squarely at kids. Nothing wrong with that, but again not challenging.

War Horse was trying emulate a glossy 1950s MGM film, which was contradictory to 2000 attitudes, and again not very challenging.

The Post and Bridge of Spies - terrific but decidedly unchallenging films.

The only film that showed some ambition was Lincoln and it's one of his late-career highlights, but that has limited world-wide appeal. 

I wouldn't say he's recovered that much either. He should have made Hamilton instead of West Side Story. Hamilton's not much more of a challenge, but it's far more relevant and would get a lot more attention than simply remaking what was already an excellent movie.

I thoroughly enjoyed Ready Player One, but it's empty entertainment - basically a kind of Who Framed Roger Rabbit? styled film but without Rabbit's good story and good performances.

The Fableman's however was just what Spielberg needed to make - a small character focused real world autobiographical movie. It was heartfelt and challenging. I think it will be well regarded as time goes by.

You said earlier that your issue with Spielberg's films is that they don't make you think.

To play devil's advocate, there are many (often beloved) styles of filmmaking that have focused on emotion and/or spectacle rather than 'ideas': MGM musicals, kung fu movies, swords and sandals epics, Ray Harryhausen fantasy adventures.

Yes, cinema can absolutely be thought-provoking and satirical and a new perspective on the world, but the sheer visceral virtuosity of a Jackie Chan or a Fred Astaire is also an important part of cinema's history and possibilities, no? 

And I'd argue that, at his best, Spielberg was certainly a virtuoso of mainstream, special effects-driven blockbuster cinema.

Understanding how our current world came to be through a historical lens can be important.  Whether The Post is successful in that endeavor is debatable but Spielberg is doing a lot more with the story than creating a time capsule. 

The Post's themes of government coverup, freedom of the press, overuse of "classified" etc. mirror the same issues we have today.

Nixon's banishment of The Post from the White House in retaliation for telling the truth isn't that far away from Trump's universal claim of "fake news".

In Ready Player One, you can't help but wonder how much he actually directed, and how much was left to assistant directors working with CGI artists. I think Spielberg's style has been drowned out by an overreliance on special fx and post-production. His films just don't *look* like Spielberg films anymore. They don't feel like Spielberg films.

Consider The Crystal Skull. A lot of people find much of it too ludicrous to bear -- Indy surviving a nuke in a fridge, or his son swinging vines with monkeys. But that kind of absurdity was not new in the franchise. The fridge is no less crazy than [jumping out of a plane with only an inflatable raft to cushion the fall](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U8x2PcmL4pg). 

I think a key difference is that, in the case of the latter, *they literally threw a raft out of a plane, and shot real footage of it falling and hitting on the snow.* They didn't just bullshit it with CGI. Now, granted, the rear-projection shots don't look great. I would say thy look as bad as swinging with monkeys on the vine. But since the shots are interspersed with real footage, there's still a strong sense of something that's been lost in the last 30 years: movie magic. The spectacle in the older films at least *looks* real, real enough for the audience to buy into it. But when you're particularly heavy with the CGI aesthetic, it looks fake, you don't buy into it, and so the spectacle comes off as silly as it sounds when being described. There's no movie magic.

(Mind, this isn't supposed to be another "CGI is the worst thing ever" rant. CGI is a tool, and like any tool, it should be used in moderation, and used *well*, e.g. Jurassic Park as an example of moderation, or Fury Road as an example of strong execution. Or, the filmmaker should just all-in, and make the entire film animated, so that there's at least a consistency in presentation, and no uncanny valley effect that we get from live action actors in transparently CGI playgrounds. Almost every single superhero film of the last 10 years, and Zack Snyder's movies in particular, can look awful times). 

Spielberg used to be an ace at spectacle, but it seems like today's toolset has robbed him of that. If he were to make Jaws today, there would be no mechanical shark (and who would blame him, the thing was a nightmare to work with). It would be a CGI shark, it would look like a CGI shark, and audiences would treat it like a CGI shark. But 50 years on, you can still look back at some moments in Jaws, and goddamn, the shit looks real, in part because *it is.* The fear it inspired at the time was real. So the old Jaws still has the movie magic. But today's Jaws wouldn't. 

So I would argue part of what Spielberg has lost is the movie magic. He just isn't pulling it off anymore. And that isn't to say it's impossible to do these days -- Everything Everywhere All at Once had a meager budget and tons of CGI, but it leverages those special fx in a way that Spielberg can't seem to, or at least, not to the degree that he could practical fx in his prime. 

That said, my rationale doesn't explain why his dramatic films hit less hard as well. It could be that Spielberg is just falling victim to [what Tarantino fears happens to all older directors](https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/quentin-tarantino-retirement-directors-horrible-last-movies-1234642019/). I'm not sure I buy that, but I do think fashion has changed over the decades, and Spielberg's style of drama, which has always been critiqued as a bit too sentimental, just works poorly in today's especially cynical age. I think there has been *some* backlash to the sarcastic 90s, insofar as more work these days have embraced earnestness (again, Everything Everywhere All At Once comes to mind), I think in Spielberg's case it comes off as so slickly produced, so *Hollywood,* that the sentimentality doesn't feel genuine. It feels manipulative. 

But I'm mostly speculating at this point. I'm open to the discussion; I may have it right, I may have it wrong. It could be decades after Spielberg's death that we finally cement his legacy as a director. It does seem like, at this point in time, his greatest impact on cinema will be the blockbuster, though, and not anything he's made since, as skillful as he has often been.
I'm not sure anyone has ever made that claim, in light of *1941*, *The Lost World: Jurassic Park*, etc.

I honestly feel like A.I. is one of his most underrated movies.
